steps: Set up a controlled plunge or tub where you can enter and exit easily, keep your head out of the water, know the approximate water temperature before you start, and use a setting where help is immediately available for early sessions if entry goes badly.

Begin with a conservative 1-to-3-minute session. Only extend toward 5 minutes on later sessions if the first minute stays controllable, exit remains easy, and you rewarm normally afterward without chest symptoms, faintness, confusion, or lingering breathing difficulty.

Enter calmly without intentional hyperventilation, breath-holding, or face immersion. Do not turn the plunge into a breathwork stack or a cold-endurance challenge. Exit early if breathing control, balance, or chest comfort are not clearly okay.
Warm back up gradually after the session, dry off, and log how quickly normal warmth and breathing return. Keep open-water swimming and face-immersion practice outside this protocol.
Log the session details and compare later-same-day stress or mood plus next-morning resting cardiovascular context against your own baseline rather than against an internet target.
stopConditions: Stop the session immediately for chest pain or pressure, palpitations, faintness, marked dizziness, confusion, collapse, new neurologic symptoms, or breathing you cannot control.
After exit, if chest symptoms, breathing difficulty, confusion, collapse, or failure to rewarm are not resolving promptly, seek urgent medical evaluation rather than treating that as adaptation.
End the experiment if you cannot enter or exit safely or if symptoms repeatedly outweigh any possible benefit.
protocol.target: controlled head-out tub or plunge immersion with easy exit and approximate water temperature known
tips: Keep time of day and session context as stable as practical so the signal is easier to read.
Treat stand-alone cold plunge and post-exercise cold plunge as different contexts even if you personally do both.
Colder or longer is not assumed to be better; the direct evidence base does not validate an extreme home target.
If you already use sauna, contrast therapy, or cold showers, either pause them or log them clearly so attribution stays honest.

researchLandscape.bottomLine: Cold Plunge is a limited-confidence healthy-adult self-experiment. The clearest direct signal is delayed stress or affect improvement, while the clearest safety signal is first-minute cold shock and cardiorespiratory risk during entry.

groups.label: Direct healthy-adult plunge evidence
groups.summary: One healthy-adult review, a few small single-session studies, and one tiny repeated-use trial support cautious self-testing of mood/stress and limited resting cardiovascular signals, but not broad promised benefits.

groups.label: Entry safety and cardiac boundaries
groups.summary: The strongest cold-plunge evidence is actually about acute hazard framing: first-minute cold shock, respiratory loss of control, blood-pressure surges, arrhythmia plausibility, and the need for screening and clear stop conditions.

groups.label: Dose and mechanistic boundaries
groups.summary: Mechanistic and boundary papers support treating cold plunge as a dose-dependent cold stressor. They help explain why colder or longer exposures raise strain, but they do not validate an extreme home target.

groups.label: Athlete recovery and training context
groups.summary: Post-exercise CWI and contrast-water papers support some soreness and delayed recovery endpoints, but they are exercise-context studies. Repeated post-resistance CWI can also trade short-term recovery against some strength-adaptation outcomes.

groups.label: Adjacent variants and public protocol claims
groups.summary: Winter swimming, cold showers, cryotherapy, and external named protocol pages help map adjacent expectations and public claims, but they should not be merged into Murph’s default cold-plunge assertions.

researchLandscape.mainCaveat: Direct plunge evidence is still small, mixed, and demographically narrow, and much of the broader cold literature belongs to adjacent variants or safety context rather than direct efficacy.
researchLandscape.primaryClaim: A conservative, controlled head-out plunge is reasonable to test for later-same-day stress or mood change, but the evidence does not justify broad benefit promises or extreme dosing.

This protocol is a bounded self-experiment, not a treatment plan or a test of willpower.

entities.summary: Use a short, controlled, head-out cold-water immersion to test whether later-same-day stress or mood improves enough to matter, while treating first-minute cold shock as the main safety problem.

notes: Use the 7-day baseline to learn your normal same-day stress and mood pattern plus resting heart rate and, if you already measure it consistently, home morning blood pressure as optional context.
During the 14-day intervention, favor three planned sessions per week instead of daily exposure so the experiment stays conservative and easy to interpret.

Manual same-day stress and mood ratings are the main user-facing outcomes. Resting heart rate is the clearest repeated-use context measure; if you already track home morning blood pressure consistently, keep it as optional context rather than a promised endpoint.
Treat HRV, sleep, soreness, and recovery metrics as exploratory notes unless you are intentionally running a separate post-exercise variant.

entities.title: Cold Plunge
whyItWorks: Cold plunge is best understood as a short, controlled cold-stress dose. The body responds first with strong autonomic and respiratory stress, not automatic relaxation. Source keys: source_artifact:pmid-33910456, source_artifact:pmid-10751106, source_artifact:pmid-36150503.

Some of the most useful direct signals appear later rather than instantly: the review backbone and one acute 10 °C study point toward delayed stress or negative-affect improvement rather than a universal immediate mood lift. Source keys: source_artifact:pmid-39879231, source_artifact:pmid-37866096.

A small repeated-exposure study suggests that after a few weeks, resting cardiovascular measures such as heart rate and mean arterial pressure may shift, while leukocyte findings remained mostly null or uncertain. Source keys: source_artifact:pmid-37711459.

Repeated exposure can blunt part of the first-minute cold-shock response after roughly four exposures, which supports conservative acclimation-first onboarding instead of a first-day maximal dose. Source keys: source_artifact:pmid-38211547, source_artifact:pmid-33276648, source_artifact:pmid-31702722.

entities.body:
## What this tests

Consistent Wake Time tests whether a stable wake/rise window makes your sleep timing more regular without stealing sleep.

The clean win is not “woke up early.” The clean win is: wake-time variability drops, enough sleep is preserved, daytime sleepiness does not worsen, and the change is not explained by travel, illness, shift work, late caffeine, alcohol, naps, or device error.

## What to compare

Use the 7-day baseline as your normal schedule. During the 28-day intervention, compare:

- wake-time variability and days inside the target window,
- total sleep time or sleep opportunity,
- daytime sleepiness or alertness,
- sleep efficiency and sleep-onset latency as secondary signals,
- and major confounders such as naps, alcohol, caffeine, light exposure, stress, illness, travel, and work or school constraints.

## Interpretation

A useful result is a repeated-window trend, not one perfect morning. If wake-time consistency improves but sleep duration drops or daytime sleepiness worsens, interpret that as a safety miss, not a successful protocol.

The research landscape is intentionally conservative. Direct evidence is small and mixed, often regularizing both bedtime and wake time. Observational regularity and social-jetlag studies are useful context, but they do not prove that this protocol prevents disease or improves long-term clinical outcomes.

## Boundaries

Do not use this protocol as sleep restriction, insomnia treatment, circadian phase treatment, or a way to push through dangerous sleepiness. When safety and regularity conflict, choose sleep and safety.

caveats: Several direct-bucket studies regularized bedtime, sleep duration, or overall sleep timing as well as wake time.
Samples were often small, short-duration, student-heavy, healthy-adult, or clinically mismatched.
claims.text: The closest intervention evidence for Consistent Wake Time is mostly broader sleep-wake or sleep-timing regularization rather than a pure wake-time-only randomized wellness trial base; adjacent wake-time-specific and fixed-wake variability sources should be used only as context.

caveats: The one-hour window is evidence-informed by schedule-regularization evidence, not optimized against other wake windows.
Adult and pediatric sleep-duration recommendations are safety boundaries, not individualized prescriptions.
claims.text: A practical default can use a chosen wake/rise window of about 60 minutes while protecting adequate sleep opportunity; this window is borrowed from broader sleep-wake regularization evidence and has not been optimized or validated as a wake-time-only dose.

caveats: No extracted source validates a Murph-specific wearable algorithm for wake-window adherence.
Sleep Regularity Index is a broader sleep-wake pattern metric and should not replace the wake-time target.
claims.text: Primary measurement should record final wake/rise time each day and summarize both wake-time variability and target-window adherence, with diary correction when wearable detection is uncertain.

caveats: These are candidate personal trend signals, not guaranteed benefits.
The intervention evidence is small and short and often regularizes broader timing than wake time alone.
Autonomic findings are mixed and should be described as short-term marker changes, not uniformly beneficial autonomic improvement.
claims.text: When sleep opportunity is preserved, defensible personal signals include lower wake-time variability and possible changes in subjective daytime sleepiness, diary sleep continuity, negative mood, or selected short-term autonomic markers.

caveats: Some null findings come from small or adjacent-variant studies and set claim boundaries rather than proving absence of any effect.
Wearable and actigraphy measures can diverge from subjective reports.
claims.text: Protocol prose should not promise improvements in EEG sleep architecture, cognition, broad mood, sleep duration, sleep efficiency, sleep quality, blood pressure, peripheral vascular function, or wearable sleep efficiency.

caveats: These sources are observational and vulnerable to residual confounding, reverse causation, selection effects, and measurement heterogeneity.
Most exposures measure broad sleep regularity or social jetlag rather than a prescribed wake-time intervention.
claims.text: Large sleep-regularity, social-jetlag, and cardiometabolic observational sources justify tracking timing regularity as context, but they do not show that a Consistent Wake Time self-experiment prevents cardiovascular events, mortality, obesity, metabolic disease, depression, anxiety, or poor academic outcomes.

caveats: Device algorithms, missing nights, naps, split sleep, illness, travel, and sensor changes can distort wake-time and sleep-continuity estimates.
Clinical sleep-disorder evaluation is outside the self-experiment.
claims.text: Consumer wearables and sleep diaries can support multi-night trend tracking, but they should not be treated as diagnostic tests or as proof that a sleep disorder has been ruled out.

caveats: Crash-risk sources are safety-boundary evidence, not efficacy evidence for the protocol.
Persistent excessive sleepiness is a clinical referral boundary.
claims.text: New or worsening daytime sleepiness, impaired vigilance, unsafe morning impairment, drowsy driving, or safety-sensitive work while short on sleep should pause or end the experiment and shift the goal back to adequate sleep and appropriate care.

caveats: Guidelines and occupational sources define boundaries and referral contexts; they do not test this self-experiment.
Bipolar-spectrum and shift-work contexts may require different timing targets or clinical/occupational fatigue-management plans.
claims.text: Chronic insomnia, suspected obstructive sleep apnea or hypersomnolence, clinician-managed circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders, bipolar-spectrum mood destabilization risk, rotating shift work, long work hours, and safety-sensitive schedules should not be folded into the default self-directed protocol.

planDefaults.firstSessionGuidance: Start with baseline logging before changing the wake target. If the chosen wake window would make tonight too short, adjust later or postpone instead of forcing it.

mustAsk.prompt: Would the proposed wake window routinely leave you short on sleep because bedtime cannot realistically move earlier?
mustAsk.why: The protocol should not become sleep restriction.

mustAsk.prompt: Are you currently having excessive daytime sleepiness, drowsy driving, unsafe morning impairment, or safety-sensitive work while short on sleep?
mustAsk.why: Safety and adequate sleep override wake-time regularity.

mustAsk.prompt: Do you have severe or chronic insomnia, loud snoring with witnessed apneas, suspected sleep apnea, narcolepsy or hypersomnolence symptoms, or another unresolved sleep-disorder concern?
mustAsk.why: These are clinical evaluation or treatment boundaries, not wake-time-only troubleshooting targets.

mustAsk.prompt: Are you dealing with rotating shifts, long work hours, jet lag, delayed sleep phase, school-start constraints, caregiving nights, or another schedule constraint that makes one daily wake window unrealistic?
mustAsk.why: The plan may need adaptation, postponement, or a different fatigue-management approach.

mustAsk.prompt: Have you had bipolar disorder, recent mania or hypomania, or mood destabilization when sleep gets shorter or timing changes?
mustAsk.why: Sleep loss and rhythm shifts can destabilize vulnerable mood states.

notes: A positive or uncertain screen is not a diagnosis; it means the self-directed default run is not the right next step without adjustment, postponement, or clinician/occupational guidance.

additionalConditions: Do not create a run when the selected wake window is expected to cause repeated short sleep.
Do not create a run when the user expects to drive or do safety-sensitive work while sleepy to hit the wake target.

startIntent.displayPrompt: Hey Murph, I want to explore a Consistent Wake Time experiment.

lineage.rationale: Default Murph wake-time-anchored regularity experiment, kept separate from bedtime-only regularity, full sleep hygiene, CBT-I fixed-rise-time care, sleep restriction, light therapy, melatonin, social-jetlag reduction, delayed sleep-wake phase treatment, and shift-work adaptation.

protocol.doseSignature: Daily · chosen 60-minute wake/rise window · protect sleep opportunity · 7-day baseline + 28-day intervention
keepInMind: This is not a treatment for chronic insomnia, sleep apnea, narcolepsy, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders, bipolar mood destabilization, or shift-work fatigue.
The strongest direct source used both bedtime and wake-time windows, so evidence for wake-time-only effects is limited.
No extracted source validates an optimal universal wake-time window, adherence percentage, weekend tolerance, or consumer-wearable algorithm.

Lower wake-time variability is the primary behavior signal; health, metabolic, cardiovascular, mortality, sleep-stage, or disease-prevention benefits should not be inferred from observational context.
logFields: estimated total sleep time or time in bed
stress, illness, travel, shift work, or schedule disruption
steps: For 7 baseline days, do not try to change your schedule; log final wake time, time out of bed, lights-out time, estimated sleep duration, daytime sleepiness, naps, and major confounders.
Choose a daily wake/rise window no wider than 60 minutes. Pick the latest window that still works with your real obligations and gives you enough sleep opportunity.
Set the wake window as a consistency target, not an exact-minute alarm. The aim is to reduce day-to-day drift while staying rested enough to function safely.
Plan bedtime backward from the wake window so the schedule preserves adequate sleep opportunity. If bedtime cannot realistically move earlier, choose a later wake window or postpone the run.
During the 28-day intervention, wake or get out of bed inside the chosen window on as many days as safely reasonable, including free days when you are not recovering from short sleep.
If you are acutely short on sleep, ill, jet-lagged, unusually sleepy, or facing safety-sensitive driving or work, prioritize sleep and safety, log the exception, and resume only when safe.
Review weekly trends in wake-time variability, days inside the window, sleep duration, sleepiness, naps, and confounders rather than judging single nights.
Safety overrides that protect sleep opportunity, illness recovery, drowsy-driving prevention, or safety-sensitive work should be logged as valid exceptions, not counted as nonadherence.
stopConditions: Pause or end the run if the wake target repeatedly reduces sleep opportunity or produces new or worsening daytime sleepiness.
Do not drive, commute, operate machinery, or do safety-sensitive work while sleepy or acutely short on sleep just to preserve the wake target.

Stop and seek appropriate guidance for persistent excessive sleepiness, loud snoring with witnessed apneas, suspected narcolepsy or hypersomnolence symptoms, severe insomnia, or unexplained sleep-disorder signs.
Stop and seek appropriate guidance for signs of mania or hypomania, unusual agitation, risky activation, or mood destabilization linked to shorter or shifted sleep.
Adapt or defer the protocol during rotating shifts, long work hours, jet lag, acute illness, caregiving nights, or other contexts where a rigid wake window is unsafe or unrealistic.
protocol.target: Wake or rise within a personally realistic 60-minute window that still allows adequate sleep opportunity.
tips: Make the first target realistic rather than aspirational; a later consistent window is safer than an early window that creates sleep debt.
Pair the wake target with a bedtime or wind-down guardrail so consistency does not silently become sleep restriction.
Use a wearable for convenience if available, but keep a simple sleep diary field for final wake time and time out of bed.
Keep caffeine timing, alcohol, late screens or bright light, naps, training load, stress, and travel as stable as reasonably possible while testing.
Weekends can use the same window when sleep opportunity is adequate, but recovery sleep wins when weekday sleep has been too short.

researchLandscape.bottomLine: Consistent Wake Time is best framed as a modest, sleep-opportunity-preserving timing experiment with limited direct evidence and a larger adjacent regularity literature.

groups.label: Direct and near-direct timing regularization
groups.summary: Short intervention sources support feasibility and some subjective or autonomic signals, but most regularize broader sleep-wake timing rather than wake time alone and preserve sleep opportunity.

groups.label: Adjacent wake-time and fixed-wake context
groups.summary: Wake-time-specific daily behavior and fixed-wake variability studies inform measurement and plausible short-term signals, but they do not establish causal wake-time-only efficacy.

groups.label: Measurement, diary, and wearable context
groups.summary: Measurement sources support tracking final awakening, time out of bed, wake-time variability, sleep regularity, and diary/wearable caveats; they do not make consumer devices diagnostic.

groups.label: Sleep-regularity observational context
groups.summary: Cohort and review literature links irregular sleep timing with academic, mental-health, cardiovascular, mortality, and cardiometabolic outcomes, but these associations are not causal protocol evidence.

groups.label: Social jetlag, youth, and school constraints
groups.summary: Social-jetlag and adolescent sources inform workday/free-day mismatch, school-start constraints, and population mismatch; they should not be converted into adult wake-time-only efficacy claims.

groups.label: Clinical, sleepiness, driving, and shift-work boundaries
groups.summary: Guidelines, sleep-duration consensus, drowsy-driving evidence, circadian and hypersomnolence guidance, bipolar/social-rhythm literature, and shift-work sources define stop conditions and referral boundaries.

researchLandscape.mainCaveat: No extracted source establishes a pure wake-time-only protocol as a treatment for insomnia, disease prevention, metabolic risk, cardiovascular risk, mortality, or sleep-stage improvement.
researchLandscape.primaryClaim: The most defensible target is improved wake-time regularity, with possible short-term subjective sleepiness or diary-continuity benefits in people whose current schedule is irregular.

entities.summary: Choose a realistic daily wake/rise-time window and keep it stable while protecting enough sleep, then test whether wake-time regularity and daytime sleepiness or alertness signals improve.

notes: Treat wake-time variability and target-window adherence as the primary behavior outcomes.
Track total sleep time or sleep opportunity and daytime sleepiness as safety guardrails; do not count short-sleep success as a clean win.
Sleep efficiency, sleep-onset latency, and HRV are secondary or exploratory context signals with mixed and confounded evidence.
Use the same wearable and diary method across baseline and intervention when possible; manually correct obvious wake-time detection errors.
The 7-day baseline and 28-day intervention are Murph-pragmatic defaults, not source-validated optimum lengths.
Interpret the 20/28 minimum only after separating unsafe or medically appropriate safety overrides from ordinary missed adherence days.

entities.title: Consistent Wake Time
whyItWorks: Wake time is a practical anchor for sleep timing regularity; the direct evidence base uses broader sleep-wake regularization and short regular-timing interventions rather than a pure wake-time-only trial base. Source keys: source_artifact:pmid-8843535, source_artifact:doi-10.1111/j.1479-8425.2011.00524.x, source_artifact:pmid-40543253.

Protecting sleep opportunity is the mechanism guardrail: a stable wake window is only useful when it does not create chronic short sleep or daytime impairment. Source keys: source_artifact:pmid-8843535, source_artifact:pmid-26039963, source_artifact:pmid-27250809, source_artifact:pmid-37684151.

Regularity metrics, diaries, and wearables can make the behavior visible over repeated nights, but measurement sources require diary correction and caution against diagnostic interpretations. Source keys: source_artifact:pmid-22294820, source_artifact:pmid-33864369, source_artifact:pmid-29734997, source_artifact:pmid-38149978.

attribution.note: Drafted from the creatine-monohydrate research run using the normalized source-page drafts, canonical source ledger, atomic findings, and section syntheses listed in the package research context.

entities.body:
Creatine monohydrate is the canonical Murph creatine protocol for screened adults who want a practical, trackable supplement experiment around resistance training, repeated high-intensity work, body-weight changes, and tolerance.

## How to run it

Use plain creatine monohydrate daily. The default path is **3–5 g/day without loading**. Loading is optional: use **no more than 20 g/day split into four separated 5 g-or-smaller servings for 5–7 days**, then continue with 3–5 g/day. Take it at a repeatable time; with a meal is fine if it helps adherence, but strict post-workout timing and high-sugar co-dosing are not required. Sources: source_artifact:pmid-8828669, source_artifact:pmid-12660409, source_artifact:pmid-20609257, source_artifact:pmid-23919405, source_artifact:pmid-34610729, source_artifact:pmid-36465581, source_artifact:pmid-35010653, source_artifact:pmid-8944667, source_artifact:pmid-10956365, source_artifact:pmid-20035494.

## What to measure

The strongest practical read is not “did creatine make everything better?” It is whether a repeatable training endpoint, training volume, body-weight context, and tolerance changed while training and diet stayed stable enough to interpret. Good endpoints include repeated strength outputs, reps at a fixed load, total tonnage, repeated sprint/power work, body weight, GI symptoms, adherence, and perceived recovery as context. Sources: source_artifact:pmid-40944139, source_artifact:pmid-41328071, source_artifact:pmid-39074168, source_artifact:pmid-36041731, source_artifact:pmid-18373286.

## What the evidence supports

The research base is most useful for healthy-adult resistance-training and repeated high-intensity contexts. It supports a reasonable experiment around selected strength, training-volume, lean-mass/fat-free-mass, and repeated high-intensity endpoints, while preserving null or mixed findings for some strength tests, peak-power/fatigue/lactate endpoints, swimming/endurance contexts, fat-loss interpretations, and subgroup claims. Sources: source_artifact:pmid-39074168, source_artifact:pmid-40944139, source_artifact:pmid-36041731, source_artifact:pmid-39441446, source_artifact:pmid-36877404, source_artifact:pmid-37892421.

## Safety posture

For studied healthy adults using plain monohydrate in protocolized doses, the safety record is generally reassuring but not risk-free. Split larger doses, track GI symptoms and body-weight changes, and get clinician guidance for kidney disease or abnormal labs, pregnancy/lactation, minors, bipolar/mania risk, muscle disorders, disease-treatment use, nephrotoxic co-exposures, or non-monohydrate products. Sources: source_artifact:pmid-40198156, source_artifact:pmid-41199218, source_artifact:pmid-18373286, source_artifact:pmid-19295968, source_artifact:pmid-24766646, source_artifact:pmid-41558805, source_artifact:pmid-36000773.

## Boundaries

This page should not be used as proof that creatine improves cognition, endurance, fat loss, bone density, Parkinson disease, mental health, pregnancy outcomes, pediatric performance, or every sport outcome. It also should not collapse creatine HCl, ethyl ester, buffered creatine, nitrate, chelates, liquid serums, or multi-ingredient products into monohydrate. Sources: source_artifact:doi-10.2903-j.efsa.2024.9100, source_artifact:govuk-creatine-cognitive-function-2024-08-14, source_artifact:pmid-38582412, source_artifact:pmid-39070254, source_artifact:pmid-36000773, source_artifact:pmid-19228401.

## Research-run notes

This landing draft uses 298 normalized source-page drafts from 11 extraction batches. The canonical ledger contains 303 records; five were non-source-page context rows. No source-extraction run processed more than 40 source records; the largest recorded extraction batch contains 38 records.

caveats: Muscle-store and biopsy endpoints are not the same as user-facing strength, body-composition, or symptom outcomes.
Some direct loading evidence is small, male-only, or has incomplete participant-count extraction.
ODS and ISSN dosing language is background guidance, not a direct head-to-head loading trial.
claims.text: A rapid loading option is evidence-supported for raising muscle creatine stores quickly: direct physiology studies used repeated 5 g doses or 20 g/day-style loading, while background guidance commonly frames rapid loading as no more than about 20 g/day split into four separated 5 g-or-smaller servings for 5–7 days or about 0.3 g/kg/day for 5–7 days.

caveats: The trained-cyclist 3 g/day trial increased muscle stores but did not improve final sprint performance versus placebo.
Gradual dosing is slower than loading; it should be presented as a lower-burden alternative, not a faster approach.
Exact saturation timing varies by dose, body size, baseline stores, diet, and training context; extraction does not support a precise individual saturation date.
claims.text: Loading is optional: direct evidence and guidance support a slower no-load strategy in which lower daily creatine dosing raises muscle stores over weeks, including 3 g/day for 28 days increasing resting muscle total creatine and creatine phosphate in trained cyclists.

caveats: The 2 g/day and 5 g/day maintenance finding came from a small male physiology sample.
The evidence supports a practical range, not a single universally optimal maintenance dose.
Larger-athlete dose guidance appears in background position-stand material and should not be treated as a direct dose-response RCT result.
claims.text: After loading, ongoing maintenance dosing should be used if the goal is to keep stores elevated: direct physiology evidence found that 2 g/day and 5 g/day preserved post-loading total creatine for 6 weeks, while 0 g/day declined; practical guidance commonly uses 3–5 g/day as the maintenance anchor.

caveats: Washout detail comes from a small male physiology study.
The extraction does not establish a universal washout duration for all users.
This is mainly a design guardrail for crossover tests and interpretation, not a dosing benefit claim.
claims.text: For self-experiment design, the page should distinguish a fast loading window from slower no-load saturation and should avoid assuming immediate washout: one direct extraction found the no-maintenance group had not fully returned to baseline muscle total creatine by 6 weeks after loading.

caveats: The post-workout-favorable trial was small, short, male-only, and lacked a placebo group.
The modern pre/post RCT co-ingested whey and maltodextrin and had attrition.
The morning/evening study was small, elite-sport-specific, and had no placebo arm in the extracted timing comparison.
claims.text: Creatine timing should be flexible rather than mandatory: one small direct study directionally favored post-workout dosing, but later direct pre/post studies found no clear timing advantage, and a morning-versus-evening study in elite female handball players did not show a clear absolute time-of-day advantage.

caveats: The exercise-proximity evidence is physiology-focused and does not directly measure long-term training outcomes.
The acute carbohydrate/exercise retention design is not the same as ordinary consumer meal timing.
Use this claim to prevent overclaiming, not to deny that users may prefer post-workout dosing for routine reasons.
claims.text: Exercise-proximity physiology supports plausibility for uptake around exercise, but it should not be converted into a rule that creatine must be taken immediately after every workout: one-legged exercise promoted creatine and glycogen accumulation, while another acute design found no additional retention difference between carbohydrate groups with versus without prior exercise.

caveats: Most positive co-ingestion findings are acute retention or uptake endpoints, often in small male samples.
Some carbohydrate protocols used large sugar loads that may reduce practicality or tolerance.
The body-composition moderator result may be underpowered, and protocol details varied.
claims.text: Carbohydrate or protein/carbohydrate co-ingestion can improve creatine retention or muscle accumulation in acute physiology studies, but the protocol should make co-ingestion optional because extracted performance and body-composition evidence does not show that high-sugar or protein/carbohydrate co-dosing is required or clearly superior.

caveats: Detailed allocation and participant count were not available for the main GI-dose extraction.
The single-bolus-above-5 g note is dossier-level context, not a primary adverse-event trial.
Splitting may reduce risk but does not guarantee absence of nausea, diarrhea, belching, or abdominal symptoms.
claims.text: For loading or any daily intake above a single 5 g serving, dose splitting is a practical safety/tolerability guardrail: extracted safety-boundary evidence reports GI complaints during creatine use, suggests 10 g/day split into two 5 g doses was not associated with detrimental GI effects while 10 g as a single serving may increase diarrhea risk, and flags large single boluses as a GI-distress risk.

caveats: Adherence itself was not directly measured in the extracted findings.
This is an implementation synthesis from timing, co-ingestion, and GI-tolerance evidence.
It should be phrased as a practical guardrail, not as a proven adherence intervention.
claims.text: Because timing and co-ingestion evidence is not strong enough to mandate a precise schedule, the user-facing implementation should prioritize repeatable daily intake: use a fixed time or regular meal if it improves adherence, avoid requiring high-sugar co-dosing, and split larger doses only when loading, tolerability, or preference calls for it.

caveats: The 2026 3 g/day versus 5 g/day trial is small and endpoint-specific.
The dose-subgroup extraction for source_artifact:pmid-41328071 is low confidence and lacks fully extracted subgroup estimates.
Use this as an overclaim guardrail, not as evidence to personalize dosing from the extracted corpus.
claims.text: The evidence supports a practical maintenance range rather than a single universally optimal dose: extracted syntheses and trials include heterogeneous dose ranges, endpoint-specific 3 g/day versus 5 g/day findings, and low-confidence subgroup signals that should not be overread.

caveats: Use endpoint-specific phrasing; do not imply every strength test improves.
Older-adult, active-female, and subgroup effects should be stated as population-bound.
Training program, dose, duration, and baseline training status vary across included studies.
claims.text: Strength outcomes are the most defensible primary performance endpoints for creatine monohydrate experiments: syntheses report positive effects for bench/chest press, squat, overall strength, and older-adult resistance-training lean/strength outcomes, but handgrip, leg press, aged upper-extremity strength, and active-female strength/power endpoints are not uniformly positive.

caveats: Much of the direct training-volume evidence is small, male, or task-specific.
A null result under equalized training conditions should not be converted into a broad creatine-null claim.
Track actual completed reps, sets, tonnage, rest intervals, and session RPE rather than only final 1RM.
claims.text: Training volume, repeated-set work, and high-intensity intermittent work capacity are useful experiment endpoints, but effects are not guaranteed: small direct trials and overreaching designs show improved or maintained work capacity, while equalized periodized resistance training and short loading-only isokinetic torque studies found no clear advantage for several volume or torque outcomes.

caveats: Repeated-sprint benefits are more defensible for mean power/work than for peak power or fatigue index.
Short loading protocols can add body mass, which may help or hurt sport-specific outputs.
Sport-specific null evidence in running and swimming should remain visible.
claims.text: Repeated-sprint mean power and short-rest high-intensity work have a positive signal, but peak power, fatigue index, lactate, running sprint, swimming, and active-female anaerobic outcomes are mixed or often null; protocols should track mean power/work, peak power, fatigue, and body mass separately.

caveats: Early scale or lean-mass changes can reflect water shifts.
BIA and DXA lean-mass estimates are hydration-sensitive.
One 13-week trial found an early lean-body-mass wash-in difference but no added between-group lean-mass gain after 12 weeks of resistance training.
The 143-study body-composition synthesis is adjacent because not all studies were necessarily monohydrate-only.
claims.text: Body weight and lean-mass or fat-free-mass estimates should be tracked, but interpreted as hydration-sensitive proxies rather than proof of new contractile tissue: syntheses show body mass, fat-free mass, or lean body mass increases, while isotope, total-body-water, DXA, and BIA findings show water-related shifts and regional hypertrophy evidence is small or null-compatible.

caveats: Do not present creatine as a fat-loss protocol.
Prefer waist, body weight, and repeated body-composition conditions over single noisy body-fat-percentage readings.
Training and diet co-interventions likely matter.
claims.text: Fat loss should not be a primary creatine monohydrate endpoint: some resistance-training syntheses show small reductions in body-fat percentage or fat mass, but other pooled analyses found no significant fat mass, BMI, or body-fat-percentage effects, and body-fat percentage can fall when lean or water mass rises.

caveats: Label perceived recovery as exploratory or community outcome unless a direct validated-scale finding is added.
Several recovery findings involve carbohydrate co-ingestion, eccentric damage, or lab physiology rather than routine training recovery.
Do not infer guaranteed soreness or readiness improvement.
claims.text: Perceived recovery can be logged as an exploratory user endpoint, but the extraction did not recover a direct quantitative perceived-recovery effect; the better-supported recovery-adjacent evidence is physiological or task-specific, including glycogen supercompensation, muscle-force recovery after eccentric damage, and mixed fatigue-index/HRV findings.

caveats: The extraction did not recover one reliable pooled GI-event incidence estimate.
Some GI evidence is safety-boundary, observational, dossier, or co-ingestion context rather than direct monohydrate-only RCT evidence.
Track timing, dose per serving, co-ingested caffeine/protein/carbohydrate, and whether symptoms resolve with smaller divided doses.
claims.text: GI tolerance and unwanted weight gain should be tracked as usability and safety endpoints: extracted direct and safety-boundary sources include gastrointestinal irritation, abdominal symptoms, nausea, diarrhea, stomach upset, belching, and withdrawals for undesirable weight gain, while dose-splitting evidence and safety reviews suggest larger single doses are more likely to cause GI upset.

caveats: Do not collapse recreational, elite, female, older, vegetarian/vegan, swimmer, and field-sport evidence into a single expected effect.
Diet-related muscle-creatine increases are mechanistically relevant but are not sufficient evidence for sprint-performance improvement.
Sport outputs can be affected by body-mass gain.
claims.text: Outcome expectations should be population- and sport-specific: active-female evidence is mixed, some sex subgroup summaries are underpowered or non-significant, swimmer and highly trained sprint-running evidence is null, and vegetarian/vegan tissue-creatine or lean-mass increases may not translate into repeated-sprint power.

caveats: Safety review sources aggregate heterogeneous doses, durations, products, and populations.
Adverse-event reporting and ascertainment vary across trials and external databases.
This does not clear users with renal disease, pregnancy, pediatric status, bipolar/mania risk, or nephrotoxic co-exposures for unsupervised use.
claims.text: In studied populations, creatine monohydrate at recommended or protocolized doses is generally well tolerated, but this should be framed as evidence from screened or heterogeneous studies rather than a guarantee for every user.

caveats: Do not quote 2019 pooled statistics without full-text verification because the extraction flagged public-snippet inconsistency.
Most controlled renal studies were short-to-moderate duration and not CKD self-experiment studies.
A creatinine rise still deserves medical interpretation if unexpected, large, symptomatic, or paired with abnormal urine markers or low GFR.
claims.text: Creatine can raise serum creatinine or creatinine-based eGFR flags without proving kidney injury; when kidney status matters, interpretation should use context such as baseline labs, cystatin C or measured GFR where available, and urine albumin/protein rather than a creatinine value alone.

caveats: Diabetes, PAD, hemodialysis, and single-kidney data came from monitored clinical or case contexts and are not unsupervised-use clearance.
The renal-transplant lab-confounding case involved creatine ethyl ester, not routine monohydrate, but transplant status remains a major high-risk boundary.
The extraction does not establish a single universal lab cutoff for exclusion.
claims.text: Known kidney disease, markedly reduced eGFR, kidney transplant, dialysis, a single kidney, nephrotoxic medication or supplement stacks, or unresolved abnormal kidney labs should trigger clinician guidance rather than default home experimentation.

caveats: The dedicated GI study did not have participant count and detailed allocation recovered in the extraction.
Some adverse-event sources are cognition or Parkinson contexts, so they support watchouts rather than default efficacy claims.
Co-ingestion with whey, maltodextrin, caffeine, food timing, or other supplements can confound symptom attribution.
claims.text: GI symptoms are a real adherence and tolerability issue: diarrhea, stomach upset, belching, nausea, headache, and gastrointestinal irritation were reported in safety or trial records, and larger single servings are more likely to be troublesome than divided servings.

caveats: Weight change is not universal; one female futsal loading trial was retained as a counterexample outside this claim's main source set.
Body-composition methods such as BIA and DXA can be sensitive to water shifts.
The protocol should separate wanted lean/strength signals from unwanted scale-weight burden.
claims.text: Scale weight, fat-free-mass estimates, and total-body-water measures can rise after creatine, especially during loading; this is an expected monitoring signal, not automatically fat gain, but it can be undesirable for weight-sensitive sports or users.

caveats: ODS keeps cramps and heat-intolerance as anecdotal/uncommon watchouts, not established causal effects.
One hot-humid thermoregulation source had insufficient extracted results, so it should not be used for directional claims.
Heat, humidity, training load, illness, alcohol, and dehydration remain independent safety factors.
claims.text: Current extracted evidence does not support presenting recommended-dose creatine as a dehydration, muscle-cramping, or heat-intolerance hazard, but hydration and heat-stress advice should remain standard because controlled trials are often short, athlete-focused, and underpowered for rare heat illness.

caveats: Several cases are single-patient reports with incomplete exposure detail, no denominator, or multiple co-supplements.
They are best used to justify caution around abnormal kidney labs, not to claim a known event rate.
Controlled renal studies and case reports should be presented together, not selectively.
claims.text: Renal adverse-event case reports, including renal dysfunction, interstitial nephritis, and acute renal failure/proteinuria, exist and should not be ignored, but they cannot prove creatine monohydrate causality or quantify incidence by themselves.

caveats: Pregnancy and perinatal sources are largely narrative, translational, or preclinical-context reviews.
Youth sources emphasize limited long-term evidence and adverse-event underreporting rather than a proven harm signal.
The hypomania/mania signal came from small psychiatric RCT evidence and should be a boundary for bipolar/mania risk, not a claim about all users.
claims.text: Pregnancy or perinatal contexts, children and adolescents, inherited or inflammatory muscle disorders, and bipolar/mania-risk psychiatric contexts should be handled as separate supervised scenarios rather than default adult creatine-monohydrate self-experiments.

caveats: Some alternative-form sources are mechanistic, case-report, or market-review evidence rather than controlled harm-rate evidence.
Product purity and label accuracy are part of safety but were not quantified product-by-product in the section corpus.
This claim supports logging exact product/form, not claiming every non-monohydrate product is harmful.
claims.text: Safety language should stay monohydrate-specific: creatine ethyl ester, nitrate, buffered, chelate, and other marketed forms have different evidence, and ethyl ester in particular can elevate serum creatinine or create pseudo-renal-failure lab patterns.

caveats: This is an evidence-quality guardrail, not a claim that those trials found harm.
Small trial completion and no complaints can still be noted when extracted, but rare-event inference remains weak.
Protocol copy should invite symptom logging rather than relying only on published trial adverse-event tables.
claims.text: Many direct efficacy trials did not report or did not have extractable adverse-event detail, so the protocol should not convert absence of reported events in performance studies into proof of safety; dedicated safety sources should carry the safety section.

caveats: Several supporting sources are reviews, position stands, or fact sheets rather than new head-to-head trials.
This claim is about choosing the protocol boundary, not about proving that every monohydrate trial shows benefit on every endpoint.
Exact effects for specific alternative forms should remain tied to their primary studies.
claims.text: Creatine monohydrate should be the default protocol exposure because the extracted reviews and guideline-style sources describe it as the most studied reference form, while alternative forms have not shown consistent superiority.

caveats: Several trials are small, short, population-specific, or involve concurrent resistance training.
Some findings include within-group improvements, but the extracted evidence does not support between-form superiority.
One low-priority HCl source lacked a clean monohydrate comparator in the canonical extraction.
claims.text: Creatine hydrochloride should stay a separate adjacent formulation: extracted HCl-versus-monohydrate trials did not show a clear HCl advantage over monohydrate across short-term performance, body-composition, hormone, or oxidative-stress-marker outcomes.

caveats: These are formulation-specific findings, not a pooled estimate across all possible alternative products.
Trial windows were short to moderate and populations were limited.
Creatyl-L-leucine evidence used a muscle-creatine endpoint, not a long-term performance endpoint.
claims.text: Buffered creatine, creatine ethyl ester, and creatyl-L-leucine should not be treated as interchangeable upgrades to monohydrate: buffered creatine did not produce greater changes than monohydrate, creatine ethyl ester did not outperform monohydrate or placebo in the extracted resistance-training trial, and creatyl-L-leucine did not increase muscle creatine content when monohydrate did.

caveats: Case reports cannot estimate routine monohydrate risk.
The renal-transplant case is a major population mismatch from healthy adult monohydrate use.
Use these sources to prevent pooling ethyl ester or serum products with monohydrate, not to claim monohydrate causes the same lab pattern.
claims.text: Creatine ethyl ester and liquid serum products need separate formulation boundaries because extracted evidence raised delivery and lab-interpretation concerns: ethyl ester was associated with higher serum creatinine than monohydrate or placebo, ethyl-ester case reports described reversible creatinine elevations, and creatine serum was not shown equivalent to powder for creatine delivery or sprint-performance support.

caveats: Some adjacent-form findings are positive versus placebo, but lack a monohydrate comparator.
Some findings are mechanistic, acute, safety-only, or have incomplete arm-level extraction.
Nitrate-specific hemodynamic and safety considerations should not be collapsed into monohydrate safety claims.
claims.text: Positive or mixed results for creatine pyruvate/citrate, magnesium creatine chelate, and creatine nitrate should remain adjacent variant evidence unless a clean monohydrate comparator and arm-level attribution are available.

caveats: Some mixed-product studies report favorable outcomes, but attribution to creatine monohydrate alone is blocked.
This is a protocol-design rule derived from extraction directness and comparator limitations.
Users can still log co-ingestion; the guardrail is about evidence attribution.
claims.text: Creatine-containing blends with protein, carbohydrate, glucose, taurine, electrolytes, fat, pyruvate, or other co-ingredients should not be cited as direct creatine-monohydrate evidence unless the creatine-only effect is separable.

caveats: Retention and uptake endpoints are not the same as strength, hypertrophy, or repeated-sprint outcomes.
Some performance evidence had a null add-on finding for carbohydrate.
Co-ingestion should be logged because it can affect interpretation, but it is not enough by itself to create a superior protocol claim.
claims.text: Carbohydrate, protein, or mixed-nutrient co-ingestion can increase creatine retention or accumulation in some physiology studies, but the extracted evidence does not make high-sugar or protein co-ingestion mandatory and does not prove a consistent performance advantage.

caveats: This is a synthesis guardrail rather than a single tested trial result.
A product being labeled creatine is not sufficient to collapse it into monohydrate.
Mechanistic uptake evidence can support plausibility but should not replace clinical or performance endpoints when making protocol claims.
claims.text: Collapse an alternative creatine form into this monohydrate protocol only when the source identifies the form, creatine-equivalent dose, comparator, co-ingredients, muscle-creatine or relevant outcome data, tolerability/lab signals, and enough arm-level detail to show interchangeability or superiority without attribution confounding.

caveats: ODS and ISSN position-stand findings are background/context-only, not primary RCTs.
Resistance-training, sport, and repeated-sprint evidence should not be generalized to endurance performance or unrelated outcomes.
Large syntheses preserve null or endpoint-specific findings, including non-significant handgrip, leg press, peak power, fatigue, and lactate outcomes in some analyses.
claims.text: The default creatine-monohydrate protocol should be scoped to healthy adults and active adults, especially those doing resistance training or repeated high-intensity work, rather than to all populations or all possible endpoints.

caveats: Older-adult sources mix different exercise programs, doses, durations, and endpoints.
Older-female findings are context-only by canonical classification.
Bone mineral density findings are null or mixed and should not be folded into the default protocol.
claims.text: Older-adult evidence supports creatine mainly as a training-linked subgroup context: lean tissue mass and some strength endpoints improve in several resistance-training syntheses, but effects are endpoint-specific and should not be generalized to all older adults, bone health, frailty, or disease treatment.

caveats: Female-athlete dosing guidance is from a position stand, not one direct RCT.
The lifespan review is narrative and explicitly leaves pregnancy/lactation safety unresolved.
Subgroup effects by sex in the 2025 strength synthesis were extracted as smaller or non-significant in females, but exact subgroup estimates were not extracted for every endpoint.
claims.text: Adult women and female athletes should remain inside the healthy-adult scope, but the page should acknowledge that female-specific evidence is smaller and life-stage variables matter; pregnancy, postpartum, lactation, and menopause should be handled as boundary contexts rather than default protocol claims.

caveats: The vegetarian weight-training source did not recover participant count or duration.
The vegan/vegetarian sprint study was very small and found tissue/body changes without repeated-sprint improvement.
A cognition RCT did not show extra benefit by vegetarian status in the extracted summary.
Training-status subgroup difference was not statistically significant in the dose-response meta-analysis.
claims.text: Vegetarian/vegan status and training status may modify response, but the extracted evidence does not support a simple claim that vegetarians, vegans, or experienced lifters always respond more.

caveats: Some small youth athlete studies reported performance benefits, but canonical extraction marks them context-only/adjacent for an adult protocol.
Absence of reported adverse events in youth studies may reflect limited reporting rather than proof of no risk.
Under-18 use should require parent/guardian and qualified clinician or sports-dietitian oversight if discussed at all.
claims.text: Children, adolescents, and youth athletes should be outside the default adult self-experiment scope; the extracted youth literature is thinner than adult evidence, mixes sport and clinical settings, and has long-term safety and adverse-event reporting gaps.

caveats: Pregnancy evidence was extracted as safety-boundary material, not protocol efficacy evidence.
The women’s lifespan review states that pregnancy, postpartum, lactation, and menopause sections include limited/mechanistic evidence.
No direct lactation supplementation trial was extracted in the allowed finding set.
claims.text: Pregnancy, postpartum, lactation, fetal, and neonatal contexts should trigger clinician guidance and remain off-scope for the default protocol because the extracted evidence is mechanistic, translational, preclinical, or limited rather than routine healthy-adult efficacy/safety evidence.

caveats: Cognition endpoints are not evidence for strength, hypertrophy, repeated sprint, water-weight, or renal-safety outcomes.
Some cognition syntheses include disease subgroups, acute high-dose protocols, dietary-intake associations, or heterogeneous dosing.
Older-adult cognition evidence includes observational dietary-intake studies and should not be synthesized as causal supplementation evidence.
claims.text: Cognition-only literature should be quarantined as adjacent evidence: some reviews report memory or timed-task signals, but regulatory reviews did not establish a cause-and-effect cognitive-function claim and other reviews/RCTs preserve mixed or null findings.

caveats: Bone studies are mainly postmenopausal, older-women, osteopenia, or long-duration exercise-program contexts.
Concurrent training and bone endpoints prevent direct use for default protocol synthesis.
Neutral lab safety in one older osteopenic-women trial does not provide broad adverse-event rates.
claims.text: Bone-only and postmenopausal bone-health studies belong in a separate variant or context note, not the default protocol; extracted studies include small positive geometry/femoral-neck signals but larger or newer trials preserve null primary BMD findings.

caveats: Disease populations, dosing, endpoints, co-treatments, and risk-benefit thresholds differ from healthy-user supplementation.
Clinical benefit in one disease subgroup should not be generalized to unrelated conditions or healthy adults.
Psychiatric and neuromuscular disease contexts require medical supervision.
claims.text: Clinical disease-treatment literature should not be used to sell healthy-adult creatine supplementation; extracted disease sources include muscular-dystrophy subgroup benefit, metabolic-myopathy nulls, McArdle high-dose worsening, Parkinson null results including a large futility-stopped trial, and mixed psychiatric evidence with a hypomania/mania signal.

caveats: The older strength meta-analysis is classified as same-mechanism/context-only, so use it as quality context rather than the main protocol proof.
The 2025 strength/power synthesis supports selected endpoints but also includes null endpoints and incomplete subgroup details.
claims.text: The evidence base is usable but not uniformly high quality: creatine-monohydrate effects are supported by RCT meta-analyses, but older strength evidence had weak trial-quality reporting, a 2024 body-composition meta-analysis found risk-of-bias concerns in about half of included studies, and a 2025 strength/power synthesis showed endpoint-specific heterogeneity and subgroup limits.

caveats: Loading and saturation findings are not the same as long-term user-visible outcomes.
Washout data come from a small physiology study in physically active men.
claims.text: Most directly relevant efficacy evidence is short-term: common loading and repeated-sprint evidence often spans 3-7 days, adult strength evidence commonly spans 4-12 weeks, and muscle-creatine maintenance/washout physiology suggests that crossover or N-of-1 experiments need washout caution; these data do not establish long-term disease, longevity, or permanent body-composition effects.

caveats: Some positive findings are training-adjunct findings, not isolated supplement-only findings.
No-training or loading-only trials can be informative for boundaries but should not erase resistance-training evidence.
claims.text: Training context is a major confounder: many supportive outcomes are creatine plus resistance training or sport-specific training, while equalized training volume, overreaching designs, no-training designs, or short loading-only tests can produce mixed or null results; the protocol should ask users to keep training volume and program structure stable and log meaningful changes.

caveats: Do not turn co-ingestion into a required protocol rule.
Keep protein, energy intake, meat/creatine intake, and deliberate carbohydrate strategies stable during the self-experiment.
claims.text: Diet and co-ingestion can confound interpretation: glucose or carbohydrate co-ingestion affected muscle uptake in physiology work and was part of a responder-dependent resistance-training trial, but carbohydrate co-ingestion did not clearly enhance pooled body-composition effects; at least one modern trial also noted incomplete capture of dietary creatine intake.

caveats: Sparse or non-significant female subgroup findings may reflect low power, not proof of no effect.
Older-adult and female-athlete position-stand material should not be converted into broad unsupervised efficacy claims.
claims.text: Generalizability is limited: positive strength and body-composition evidence often skews toward adults under 50, younger or male samples, athletes, or active adults; female-specific and older-adult subgroup evidence is smaller, mixed, or limited by reporting gaps, so age and sex boundary language should be explicit.

caveats: Endurance, aquatic sport, and cognition sources are classified as adjacent, background, or context-only where applicable.
Use them to set boundaries, not to define the default creatine-monohydrate success metric.
claims.text: Do not generalize creatine-monohydrate evidence to endurance, swimming, or cognition as default outcomes: extracted syntheses found null endurance and swimming results, and regulatory cognitive reviews found that cause-and-effect relationships were not established under the evaluated claim conditions, with dose and population mismatch concerns.

caveats: This is not a claim that GI symptoms are common at all doses.
Absence of adverse-event extraction in small trials should not be treated as proof of absence.
claims.text: Adherence and tolerability evidence is uneven: weight gain or water retention is common enough to track, GI symptoms can occur especially with larger single boluses, and several small direct trials did not report or extract adverse-event details; tolerability should be monitored rather than assumed from efficacy trials.

caveats: Do not make post-workout dosing mandatory for the default protocol.
Timing comparisons are not the same as placebo-controlled efficacy estimates.
claims.text: Timing rules should remain flexible: timing reviews found suggestive post-exercise lean-mass signals, but strength timing effects were not clear, the pooled timing evidence was small and heterogeneous, and narrative reviews state that current evidence does not support a strict timing prescription.

caveats: Scale weight is a confounded signal during creatine use.
Lean-mass and body-fat-percentage changes should be interpreted alongside strength, training, diet, and waist or visual context.
claims.text: Body-composition interpretation needs measurement caveats: short-term body-mass gain can occur without a performance gain, fluid shifts may vary by menstrual-cycle or hormonal-contraceptive context, and some fat-percentage signals do not necessarily mean clear absolute fat-mass loss.

planDefaults.firstSessionGuidance: Start with the no-loading 3–5 g/day path unless faster saturation is worth the extra servings and GI-monitoring burden.

mustAsk.prompt: Do you have kidney disease, kidney transplant, dialysis, a single kidney, protein or albumin in urine, unresolved abnormal creatinine/eGFR, or clinician concern about kidney function?
mustAsk.why: Kidney-risk contexts and creatinine-based lab interpretation need clinical context before unsupervised supplementation.

mustAsk.prompt: Are you pregnant, trying to become pregnant, postpartum, lactating, or under 18?
mustAsk.why: These populations are outside the default healthy-adult self-experiment boundary.

mustAsk.prompt: Do you have bipolar disorder, a history of mania or hypomania, or current psychiatric instability?
mustAsk.why: The extraction preserved psychiatric boundary evidence including a hypomania/mania signal in adjacent disease-context literature.

mustAsk.prompt: Do you have a significant muscle disorder, metabolic myopathy, McArdle disease?
mustAsk.why: Disease-treatment and muscle-disorder evidence is off-scope for the default healthy-adult protocol.

mustAsk.prompt: Are you using medications or supplement stacks that a clinician has warned may affect kidney function?
mustAsk.why: Nephrotoxic co-exposures make kidney-lab interpretation and risk management more complex.

mustAsk.prompt: Is the product creatine HCl, ethyl ester, buffered creatine, nitrate, chelate, liquid serum, or a mixed pre-workout/protein formula rather than plain monohydrate?
mustAsk.why: Alternative forms and blends are adjacent variants and should not be silently treated as the monohydrate protocol.

mustAsk.prompt: Are you trying to use creatine to treat a diagnosed medical condition, major injury, psychiatric condition, pregnancy/perinatal concern, or neuromuscular disease?
mustAsk.why: Clinical-treatment and major-condition contexts have different risk-benefit thresholds and should not be folded into the default healthy-adult protocol.

mustAsk.prompt: Is the product poorly labeled, unusually high dose, missing a clear creatine monohydrate amount per serving, or not from a source you trust?
mustAsk.why: Product identity and label clarity are part of the monohydrate protocol boundary and attribution quality.

notes: The default user is a screened adult. Positive screens do not prove harm; they change the protocol from self-experiment to clinician-guided decision.

startIntent.displayPrompt: Hey Murph, I want to explore creatine monohydrate.

lineage.rationale: Murph canonical plain-creatine-monohydrate protocol; kept separate from external named protocols, alternative creatine salts/forms, multi-ingredient products, cognition-only protocols, and clinician-supervised disease-treatment contexts.

protocol.doseSignature: 3–5 g/day creatine monohydrate ongoing; optional <=20 g/day split loading as four <=5 g servings for 5–7 days; 7-day baseline + 6-week intervention
keepInMind: This is a healthy-adult exercise-performance and tolerance experiment, not a default cognition, endurance, fat-loss, bone-density, pregnancy, pediatric, or disease-treatment protocol.
Scale-weight increases can reflect water or fat-free-mass changes and are not automatically fat gain or new contractile tissue.
Creatine can complicate creatinine-based kidney-lab interpretation; abnormal labs should be interpreted with clinical context rather than ignored or panicked over.
Alternative forms such as HCl, ethyl ester, buffered creatine, nitrate, citrate/pyruvate, chelates, serums, and mixed formulas should stay separate unless a specific variant is being tested.
logFields: co-ingestion with meal, carbohydrate, protein, or blend
sleep, illness, alcohol, heat exposure, or major diet changes
steps: Before starting, record a 7-day baseline for body weight, usual training performance, training volume, GI symptoms, recovery, diet changes, and current supplements.
Choose a plain creatine monohydrate product and log the exact product name, serving size, and whether it is micronized, flavored, or mixed with other ingredients.

Choose one dosing path: either skip loading and take 3–5 g once daily, or use an optional loading phase of no more than 20 g/day split into four separated servings of no more than 5 g each for 5–7 days.
After any loading phase, move to 3–5 g/day maintenance dosing.
Take the dose at a time you can repeat. Taking it with a regular meal is acceptable if it helps adherence, but high-sugar co-ingestion and strict post-workout timing are not required.
Split any dose above 5 g, and split loading servings across the day rather than taking one large bolus.
Keep the training plan, protein/energy intake, caffeine/alcohol pattern, and other supplements as stable as reasonably possible during the test window.
Track repeated strength or power outputs under similar conditions rather than relying only on one best workout or a scale-weight change.
Weigh under similar conditions and interpret early weight or lean-mass changes as hydration-sensitive unless paired with stronger body-composition and performance context.

Pause or seek clinician guidance if the safety screen, symptoms, abnormal kidney labs, pregnancy/lactation, pediatric status, bipolar/mania risk, kidney disease, or a non-monohydrate product makes the default adult protocol a poor fit.
stopConditions: Stop and seek appropriate care for severe allergic-type symptoms, severe or persistent vomiting or diarrhea, fainting, chest pain, severe weakness, dark urine with muscle pain,.

Pause the experiment and get clinician guidance for unexpected abnormal kidney labs, known kidney disease, transplant, dialysis, single-kidney status, unresolved proteinuria/albuminuria, or nephrotoxic medication/supplement stacks.
Do not continue unsupervised if pregnancy, lactation, pediatric status, bipolar/mania risk, significant muscle disorder, or disease-treatment use applies.
Stop or reduce/split dosing if GI symptoms, headaches, unwanted weight gain, or adherence burden makes the experiment not worth continuing.
protocol.target: Plain creatine monohydrate, taken consistently; avoid blending evidence from other creatine forms or multi-ingredient products.
tips: Use the no-loading path when simplicity or GI tolerance matters more than fast saturation.
Use optional loading only when faster saturation is worth the extra servings and logging burden.
Post-workout dosing is fine if convenient, but consistency matters more than the clock.
A small scoop is easy to forget; pair it with a repeatable daily routine.
For a fair experiment, keep resistance training or high-intensity sessions consistent enough that changes are not just a new training-program effect.
